endorsements.title: Action Guide: Artificial Intelligence (AI)
endorsements.issuer: National Association of Community Health Centers
endorsements.quote: Remember: Providers must review and approve AI-generated notes to ensure they are accurate and complete.

endorsements.title: Adoption of AI in Healthcare Delivery Systems: Early Applications and Impacts
endorsements.quote: From a clinical perspective, errors in documentation, such as attributing notes to the wrong person or ignoring critical details, pose risks.

endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: The first is automation bias, where clinicians may rely too heavily on the tool’s output without verifying the supporting evidence from the actual clinical record. This blind acceptance of retrieved information could lead to safety issues, especially if false positives (hallucinations) are present. This concern should be addressed in the considerations.

endorsements.title: Ethical Considerations of Using ChatGPT in Health Care
endorsements.quote: Health care professionals should ensure that AI-generated content, such as reports or recommendations, is based on evidence-based medicine and aligns with established clinical guidelines.

endorsements.title: Ethical Considerations and Fundamental Principles of Large Language Models in Medical Education: Viewpoint
endorsements.quote: Maintain a critical approach: educators and students should assess LLM-generated information critically by verifying it by reference to authoritative databases and other language models.

endorsements.title: The Utility and Implications of Ambient Scribes in Primary Care
endorsements.quote: Additionally, it must be stressed that while the clinical visit may be documented automatically, the clinician must still review the output from the ambient scribe and correct any errors or omissions.

endorsements.title: Prompt Engineering in Clinical Practice: Tutorial for Clinicians
endorsements.quote: Given the potential for hallucinations or outdated content, all LLM outputs should then be verified by cross-checking with primary literature and authoritative databases such as UpToDate or PubMed.

endorsements.title: Building a Safe and Transparent Workflow for Large Language Model (LLM)-Assisted Clinical Trials and Prediction Models: A Technical Report
endorsements.quote: Require manual verification for any claim drafted with LLM support.

endorsements.title: Confronting the Ethical Issues with Artificial Intelligence Use in Nephrology
endorsements.quote: Clinicians must remain diligent when checking the outputs of AI, e.g., by proof-reading AI-generated reports or correspondence, and avoid overreliance on its outputs (so-called automation bias), particularly when they do not match the broader context of the patient's clinical picture.

endorsements.title: Transformation of a Medical Information Department to Meet the New Healthcare Realities of the Post-Pandemic Era
endorsements.quote: AI-driven systems must therefore be trained and validated carefully to ensure compliance, and their outputs must always be subject to human verification by trained Medical Information professionals before being shared externally.

endorsements.title: Ethical considerations for multimodal artificial intelligence in healthcare
endorsements.quote: Clinicians or designated clinical reviewers should verify AI-generated or AI-assisted outputs before they are incorporated into the patient record or relied upon for care, with the verification status and reviewer identity preserved as part of the object’s metadata.

evidence.title: Generating subjective, objective, assessment, and plan (SOAP)-structured medication logs using DeepSeek-R1 through prompt engineering and multi-source clinical information
evidence.outcome: Machine scores of AI logs before vs after pharmacist review and correction
evidence.effect: After manual modification, BERT F1 increased from 0.68 ± 0.03 to 0.71 ± 0.05, P < 0.05; ROUGE also improved significantly.
evidence.quote: After manual modification, the BERT score and ROUGE of the generated text were both improved significantly (e.g. BERT F 1 increased from 0.68 ± 0.03 to 0.71 ± 0.05, P < 0.05; Figure 6 and Supplemental Figure 2 ), which suggested that this step of manual revision was essential.

evidence.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence Summaries to Facilitate Emergency Department Handoff
evidence.outcome: Clinician-rated safety concerns, omissions and mischaracterizations in AI-generated ED handoff summaries
evidence.effect: Safety concerns in 6% of 50 cases; omissions of medications, labs and other details (n=6); clinicians disagreed with AI characterizations of stability, vitals and workup (n=8).
evidence.quote: Safety concerns arose in 6% of cases, with issues including data omissions and mischaracterizations.

evidence.title: Evaluation of Socio-Technical Mechanisms Shaping AI Scribe Documentation Failures: A Netnographic Study
evidence.venue: Journal of evaluation in clinical practice
evidence.outcome: Whether clinician verification identifies and corrects AI scribe errors before they propagate
evidence.effect: Documentation problems arose through socio-technical interactions that influence whether errors are identified, corrected or carried forward. Risk depended on integration quality, governance clarity and review capacity.
evidence.quote: The findings suggest that documentation problems may arise through socio-technical interactions that influence whether errors are identified, corrected or carried forward.
evidence.sample_unit: data segments (from 952 documents across 162 Reddit threads)

evidence.title: Does a Safety-Priming Instruction Reduce Risk-Fact Omission in Psychiatric Note Summarization? A Synthetic-Vignette Study of Small Open-Weight Language Models
evidence.outcome: Omitted facts in AI psychiatric summaries
evidence.effect: Generic-prompt risk-fact omission ranged 4% to 26% across four models.
evidence.quote: Baseline (generic-instruction) risk-fact omission ranges from 4% to 26% across the four models the smallest model omits the safety-critical fact roughly one time in four.
evidence.sample_unit: synthetic psychiatric intake vignettes per condition

evidence.title: Application of generative language models to orthopaedic practice
evidence.outcome: Accuracy of LLM-generated clinical letters rated by three orthopaedic clinicians
evidence.effect: ChatGPT letters 8.7/10 (SD 0.60) vs GPT-3 7.3/10 (SD 1.41), p=0.024; both sometimes omitted key information or added guidance that was at worst inaccurate.
evidence.quote: However, both LLMs sometimes omitted key information or added additional guidance which was at worst inaccurate.

evidence.title: Using large language models to generate child-friendly education materials on myopia
evidence.outcome: Ophthalmologist-rated potential harm and correctness of LLM myopia education responses
evidence.effect: About 30% of ChatGPT 4o responses rated slightly harmful; ChatGPT 3.5 and Gemini each got 1.14% 'extremely harmful' ratings for Prompt B; authors say clinicians must review all LLM materials.
evidence.quote: Additionally, approximately 30% of the ChatGPT 4o responses were still rated as “slightly harmful.”
evidence.sample_unit: questions (each answered by 4 LLMs under 2 prompts; 280 responses per prompt)

evidence.title: The ethics of simplification: balancing patient autonomy, comprehension, and accuracy in AI-generated radiology reports
evidence.outcome: Omissions, incorrect conversions and generalizations in AI-simplified reports that could reach patients unverified
evidence.effect: At 7th grade, inaccuracies with potential to alter management: inappropriate generalization 40% (8/20), omission 35% (7/20), incorrect conversion 35% (7/20).
evidence.quote: The inaccuracy patterns identified within these 20 cases were as follows: inappropriate generalization occurred in 40% (8/20), omission in 35% (7/20), and incorrect conversion in 35% (7/20).
evidence.sample_unit: radiology reports (CT and MRI), each transformed into 17 reading-grade versions

evidence.title: Impact of an Ambient AI Scribe on Medical Student Objective Structured Clinical Examination Notes: Nonrandomized Clinical Trial
evidence.outcome: incorporation of omissions into final note
evidence.effect: In paired analysis, hybrid notes had significantly lower chief complaint scores (P=.05) with fewer fully acceptable notes than human-only notes due to automation bias.
evidence.quote: In paired analysis of QNOTE elements between human-only and hybrid notes among AI scribe participants, the largest element-level change was a decline in chief complaint scores ( P =.05) driven by fewer “fully acceptable” (16/47, 34% vs 21/47, 44.7%) and more “unacceptable” (7/47, 14.9% vs 3/47, 6.4%) hybrid notes as compared to human-only notes, respectively.

evidence.title: Patient-friendly simplification and translation of neuroradiology impressions using artificial intelligence
evidence.outcome: Clinically relevant errors in AI-simplified reports that clinician review would need to catch
evidence.effect: Major omissions, malignant hallucinations and major imprecisions occurred at low but nonzero rates (up to 5.5%, 1.0%, 6.0% in spine MRI), so authors state human oversight is necessary.
evidence.quote: The presence of major/malignant mistakes necessitates human oversight, at least in the current implementation strategy.
evidence.sample_unit: neuroradiology reports (brain MRI, head CT, spine MRI); 60 impressions translated to Spanish

evidence.title: Transcription Accuracy of Automatic Speech Recognition for Orthodontic Clinical Records
evidence.outcome: Clinically significant transcription errors that would require verification
evidence.effect: Clinically significant errors seen with all systems, ranging from 2% to 66% (GPT4oTranscribeCorrected clean; Dragon Medical One background noise).
evidence.quote: Importantly, clinically significant errors were seen with all systems, ranging from 2% to 66% (GPT4oTranscribeCorrected clean; Dragon Medical One background noise, respectively).
evidence.sample_unit: narrated orthodontic diagnostic and treatment planning summaries

evidence.title: Schema Enforcement and Structured-Output Stability in Locally Deployed LLMs for Clinical Admission-Note Editing: A Proxy-Based Pre-Deployment Evaluation
evidence.outcome: numeric content preservation in generated notes
evidence.effect: Schema-enforced median numeric-token deltas were −5, −8, and −2.5; median numeric-token preservation was 42.9%, 33.3%, and 70.0% by model.
evidence.quote: In the schema-enforced condition, median numeric-token deltas were −5 for Llama3-Med42-8B, −8 for Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct, and −2.5 for Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3.

commentary.bottom_line: Eleven sources endorse clinician verification of AI output, and ten studies show that AI notes and summaries omit, misstate, or add content, but only one small offline study tests review itself. In that study, pharmacist correction of 80 AI medication logs raised a text-similarity score from 0.68 to 0.71, which says little about whether review prevents harm to patients.

perspectives.view: One retrospective replay study of 80 medication logs tests the practice. Its outcome is a machine similarity score (BERT F1 0.68 to 0.71) rather than errors caught or patient outcomes. The design, indirect outcome, single setting, and small sample suggest very low certainty. The ten hazard studies establish the problem but do not show that verification solves it.

Hazard studies report safety concerns in 6% of 50 real ED handoff summaries, risk-fact omission of 4% to 26% in psychiatric summaries, and major omissions up to 5.5% in simplified spine MRI reports. In a study of 104 medical students, hybrid notes scored lower on chief complaint (P=.05), which the authors attributed to automation bias. This suggests review alone may miss omissions.

A qualitative analysis of 2,267 clinician forum segments found that whether scribe errors were caught or carried forward depended on integration quality, governance clarity, and review capacity. Median numeric-token preservation in generated admission notes ranged from 33.3% to 70.0% by model. This suggests reviewers may need to check numbers against source data.

The single test of the practice used non-English medication logs in China, and one hazard study translated 60 neuroradiology impressions into Spanish. No test included Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy populations. The evidence therefore does not show how verification performs for those groups.

The qualitative study linked error propagation to review capacity, and a transcription benchmark found clinically significant errors from 2% to 66% depending on system and background noise. These findings suggest the review effort needed may vary by tool and setting. No study measured how much clinician time verification requires.

In radiology reports simplified to a 7th-grade level, inaccuracies with potential to alter management included inappropriate generalization in 40% (8/20), omission in 35% (7/20), and incorrect conversion in 35% (7/20). About 30% of one model's myopia education responses were rated slightly harmful. Patients may receive flawed content if no clinician checks it first.

commentary.research_gap: No study measures whether clinician verification of AI notes or answers catches omissions, misattributions, or unsupported content before they affect care in real deployment. Studies comparing structured, source-linked review against usual review, with errors caught, review time, and patient outcomes as endpoints, would address this gap.
commentary.underserved_note: The only test of the practice used non-English medication logs in China, but it was offline and measured text similarity rather than safety. No test included Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy populations, so the benefit of verification for those groups is unknown.
